shift_sale.title: POS 4 — The Shift & the Sale
shift_sale.desc: The trading day: sign-in and the top-bar indicators, opening the shift with a counted float, building sales with stack/queue and the line markers, batches/serials/units done accurately, customers, loyalty and the credit suspension, hold versus clear and every payment method's rules, receipts, the gift voucher sale and the till lock, and closing the shift against pre-filled figures that are counted, overwritten and explained.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Signing in and reading the screen
lessons.html:
This module covers the trading day from sign-in to shift close. It is the cashier's module: if any part of this track is printed and kept at the counter, it is this one. The module's law: the shift is a sealed routine — count at open, count at close, explain every variance.

Signing in. Three ways, depending on circumstances:

• Normal. Email and password. The till loads your profile, catalogue and permissions, and opens on the first console your access row grants. A forgotten password is reset by email — the terminal must be online for the reset.
• Offline. Where the profile enables it, you can sign in against the terminal's stored record when the server is unreachable — provided you have signed in online on this terminal within the last seven days. The top bar shows an Offline login marker. Practical rule: sign in online at least weekly on every terminal you use, or an outage will lock you out at the worst time.
• Manager override. If offline sign-in is refused because the terminal has no record of you, a manager can sign you in on their credentials. The sales in that session are tagged for audit, and you are told so at the time.

The top bar. Learn to read these indicators — each one is either fine, something you click, or something you report:

• Online / Offline — whether the terminal can reach the back office.
• Offline login — you signed in locally; reports and server lookups wait for the connection.
• Queued — completed sales waiting to post. They are safe; they post automatically when online.
• Re-login — a cashier's stored credentials were rejected. If it names you: click it and sign in online, or your queued sales cannot post.
• Conflicts — sales held back because a batch or serial is no longer available. Click to resolve (module 8).
• Stock stale / Price stale — the local copies need refreshing. Click to sync.
• Failed — sales the back office rejected; a supervisor handles these (module 8).
• Duty — Active or Inactive, with the shift button beside it (shown where shift management is on).
• Also: store, date, time, your name and role; the envelope (Message Hub, with unread count); Sync (refresh now — hover shows when each copy last updated); the padlock (lock the till); Sign out.

The Sales Console. Products on the left with the search box above; the current order on the right. The cart header shows the customer and the item/quantity counts — and, where credit checking is on, the customer's balance and limit. The footer shows sales total, discount, subtotal, tax, delivery fee if enabled, and net total, with the payment buttons beneath. The sidebar lists the consoles your row grants. Below it: card/list view (list fits more), product images on or off (off is noticeably faster), items per row, and Recent receipts for quick reprints.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Opening the shift
lessons.html:
Where shift management is enabled, you must open a shift before you can sell. Opening takes two minutes; doing it properly is what makes the end of the day painless.

Procedure.

1. Click the clock icon in the top bar. The Open Shift window appears.
2. Count the float — physically count the money in the drawer.
3. Enter the counted amount against each payment method. Cash is normally the only one with an opening amount; leave the others at zero.
4. Add an opening note if anything is unusual — a short float, a missing key.
5. Click Open Shift. The Duty indicator turns Active.

Why the count matters. The opening amount is what your closing count will be measured against. If you type a round number instead of counting — entering 20,000 because that is what the float should be, when the drawer actually holds 19,400 — then even a perfect day ends 600 short, and the evening is spent investigating a shortage that never happened. Worse, if that becomes normal, real shortages hide inside the always-a-bit-off habit. Thirty seconds of counting buys an evening of certainty. Note: a short float declared in the opening note is context; the same shortfall discovered at close is a dispute.

Float preparation. The float should be prepared before the shift — counted denominations suitable for change-making, sealed until the drawer is loaded. Preparing floats is a supervisor task on module 8's calendar; counting what you receive is yours.

Handover during the day. When one cashier hands a till to another mid-day, run it as two shifts: the first cashier closes their shift with a full count; the second opens a new shift with their own count. Never pass one open shift between people — a shared shift produces a shared variance, and a shared variance cannot be attributed to anyone. One person, one shift, one drawer, one count.

If a shift was never opened. Sales rung with no shift open are not attached to any shift, which is why they later seem to be missing from shift summaries. The repair is the back-office orphaned transactions tool, which attaches them to the shift they belong to — a supervisor task, and a correction, not a normal workflow. If you find yourself selling and Duty shows Inactive, stop and open a shift first.

Summary. Count before you open. Declare anything unusual in the note. Handover means two shifts. Never sell without a shift open.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Building a sale
lessons.html:
Items go into the cart three ways, and the cart has a small set of rules worth knowing precisely.

Adding items.

• Scan the barcode. The item goes straight into the cart — the search box does not need to be selected first, so scanning works even mid-conversation.
• Search by name, code or brand, then pick from the results.
• Tap a tile in the product grid.

Stack or queue. Where the profile enables the item queue option, a toggle beside the search box selects the behaviour: stack — re-scanning an item increases its existing line; queue — every scan makes its own line, used where each unit needs its own serial or batch entry.

Editing quantities. Each line has minus and plus buttons and an editable quantity box. Type the number and press Enter to apply it; press Escape to abandon the edit. Use the keys — a half-typed quantity left unconfirmed is how a wrong quantity rides through to payment.

Removing lines. The bin icon removes a line. Exceptions with fixed behaviour:

• Bonus items (from promotions), bundle components, and gift voucher lines have fixed quantities and cannot be edited line by line.
• Bundle components cannot be removed individually — remove the bundle's main line, and the components go with it. The bundle price governs its parts (module 5 covers bundles).

Line markers. Small labels on cart lines record what has happened to them:

• Bundle — the line heads a bundle.
• Rate override — the price was manually changed. Visible on review, deliberately.
• Customer discount — a discount recorded on the customer's record applied automatically.
• Batch assigned — batches have been selected for the line (clickable — see Chapter 4).

Read the markers before taking payment: a line carrying a promotion will refuse a manual discount, and the marker tells you why before the error message does. Supervisors read the same markers when reviewing sales.

Before payment: the ten-second check. Glance at the footer — item count, quantity count, net total — against what is on the counter and what the customer expects. On multi-unit items, check the unit (Chapter 4). Read any markers you did not put there yourself. A wrong quantity caught in the cart costs a keystroke; caught at payment it costs a correction; caught after the customer leaves it costs a return, an approval and an explanation.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Batches, serials and units of measure
lessons.html:
Items tracked by batch or serial, and items sold in more than one unit, add a step to the sale. The step is quick — and it is the whole point of the tracking.

Batch-tracked items. When you add a batch-tracked item, the till asks which batch the goods come from, showing available batches and quantities.

• A quantity can be split across batches — allocate part against one batch, part against another.
• Where the profile enables auto-allocate, the till picks batches for you, oldest first, and only asks when the quantity cannot be covered from one batch.
• Reducing a line's quantity releases batch allocations in reverse order — the last-allocated batch is released first.
• The Batch assigned marker on the line is clickable: use it to review or change the selection before payment.

Practical rule: make sure the batches on the sale match the goods actually going into the bag. With auto-allocate on, the till picks the oldest batch — if you physically picked from the front of the shelf, click the marker and correct it. Expiry tracking only works when the record and the bag agree.

Serial-numbered items. Serial-tracked items require one serial per unit, scanned or typed into the serial window. The line cannot proceed to payment until every unit has a serial.

Practical rule: scan the serials from the units in the bag — the actual items being handed over — never from a convenient box on the shelf. The serial ties this physical unit to this sale; warranty claims, returns and recalls all depend on that link being true. A serial record that does not match the goods handed over is worse than no record.

Units of measure. Where an item sells in more than one unit (each, pack, carton), the till asks which unit applies, and the price follows the unit chosen.

Practical rule: check the unit on multi-unit lines during the ten-second footer check. A carton sold at the single-unit price is a large, silent discount nobody approved — it looks normal on screen and only surfaces later in the margin figures.

When a batch or serial is refused. Occasionally the till refuses a batch or serial because another terminal sold it in the meantime. This is normal on a multi-till or offline estate: pick a different batch or serial and continue. If a completed sale is held back for this reason, it appears under the Conflicts indicator in the top bar; resolving conflicts is covered in module 8 — the short version is that a conflict is fixed by re-picking, and conflicts are cleared before the shift closes.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Customers, loyalty and credit at the counter
lessons.html:
A sale with no customer attached books to the walk-in customer, which is correct for most of the queue. Attach a named customer when the sale involves loyalty, credit, a delivery, or a customer who asks to be on record.

Attaching a customer. Use the person icon above the grid or the customer chip on the cart header, then:

• Search by name, phone or email and select. Offline, the search runs against the terminal's cached customer list.
• Create a new customer — name, plus mobile and email if available. Two protections from module 2 apply here: duplicate names may be refused (if the profile says so), and a new customer whose mobile number matches an existing record merges into it automatically.
• Scan a loyalty card using the scan button above the grid — the member loads automatically and their points appear on the header.

What attaching does immediately:

• Any discount recorded on the customer's record applies to the cart (the Customer discount marker) — recorded policy, applied automatically.
• Where credit checking is on, the customer's balance and credit limit appear on the cart header.

Habit: attach the customer before scanning items whenever the sale is clearly a member's or an account customer's. Attaching late still applies discounts correctly to what is in the cart, but attaching after payment is too late for points — which becomes a dispute and a reprint request together.

The credit suspension. A customer over their credit limit shows Sales suspended due to customer outstanding on the cart, and payment is blocked. Only a Power Approver holding the Credit Limit Override permission can release it — a recorded approval.

How to handle the moment: state it as the system's rule, not your judgment — the account needs a supervisor's approval before more can be added to it. If the customer prefers, a fully paid cash sale needs no release at all. Do not work around the suspension by splitting the purchase across tickets or under-recording it — module 8 treats exactly that pattern as a red flag, and the approval takes a minute.

Loyalty at the counter. Three facts:

• Earning requires attachment. A member not attached to the sale earns nothing — attaching is the programme.
• Redemption happens at payment and needs the terminal online, because the points balance lives on the server.
• Returns interact with points. If the original sale earned points that have since been spent, the return calculates what must be recovered and shows it before completion — read the figure from the screen to the customer; never estimate it (module 5 covers returns).

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Hold, clear, and taking payment
lessons.html:
Hold versus Clear. Two different actions with different consequences:

• Hold parks the basket and clears the screen for the next customer. A held basket keeps its customer, discounts and batch allocations. Resume it from the box icon above the grid, which shows the count of held baskets. Old held baskets age out automatically where the profile's housekeeping is set.
• Clear discards the basket entirely. Where the profile does not permit the cashier to clear but an approver holds the Clear Cart permission, the Clear button appears but requires an approval.

Rule: hold, do not clear. The customer who steps away to fetch a wallet gets a hold — clearing throws away the batch and serial work already done. And because building a basket, taking cash, then clearing it is a known fraud pattern, cleared carts are recorded and reviewed (module 8); the honest habit is simply to hold.

Cash. Press Cash, enter the amount tendered (or tap a quick-amount button). The till calculates and displays the change, completes the sale, opens the drawer, and prints per configuration.

Card. Without an integrated terminal, the till simply records the card amount — process the card on the machine as usual, then confirm. With an integrated terminal (module 2, Tab 5), the amount is pushed to the device and the till waits for the result.

Split payment. One bill across several methods:

1. Turn on Split payment in the payment window.
2. Choose a method and enter its portion.
3. Add another method for each further portion, watching the remaining balance fall.
4. Complete when the remaining balance reaches zero.

Over-tender rule: if cash is among the methods, over-tendering shows change due; without cash, the total cannot exceed the amount owed.

Record every portion on its true method. Recording a transfer as cash to finish faster creates two wrong figures at the close — cash over and transfer short — from one sale.

Server-verified tenders. Three tenders need the terminal online, because the balance they draw on lives on the server:

• Loyalty redemption — Redeem Loyalty Points, choose the programme, enter the points; their cash value is deducted.
• Gift vouchers — added in the payment window's voucher section, scanned or typed. More than one voucher can be applied; if vouchers cover the whole bill no other tender is needed; any surplus follows the profile's change policy.
• Store credit — chosen as a payment method; the available balance is shown, and an amount above it is refused.

Offline payment summary. Cash, manually keyed card, and transfer work offline. Integrated card, store credit, loyalty redemption, vouchers (unless Guarded Offline is configured), and any credit or part-paid sale do not — offline, collect the full amount.

Back-dating. Where the profile allows transaction date editing, a date field appears at the top of the payment window — today or earlier only. Use it only for a genuinely late-entered sale; it moves revenue between reporting days, which is why the permission is granted sparingly.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Receipts, selling a gift voucher, and locking the till
lessons.html:
Receipts. Where auto-print is on, the receipt prints on completion (one or two copies per the printer settings); otherwise print from the confirmation screen. Reprints: the Recent receipts panel (from the catalogue controls) covers the last few sales; Sales History (module 6) covers anything older.

Offline references. A sale completed offline prints its receipt with a local reference. When the sale posts, it also receives a back-office invoice number. Both numbers refer to the same sale, and a return can be found using either one. An offline receipt is a fully valid document — say so with confidence if a customer asks.

Selling a gift voucher. The procedure:

1. Tap the Gift Voucher tile on the product grid.
2. Choose a face value from the denomination buttons, or type another amount.
3. Set the quantity. Same-value vouchers group onto one line (a fixed-quantity line).
4. For pre-printed voucher stock, scan each physical card so its code binds to the value. For system-issued vouchers, leave codes blank — they are generated when the sale completes.
5. Attach a named customer — required, because the voucher may need emailing or reprinting later. If no email is on file the till prompts for one; it can be skipped, but then the printed slip is the only copy.
6. Take payment. Rule: vouchers are bought with cash-equivalent tenders only — never with another voucher, store credit, or loyalty points. Stored value cannot be used to create stored value.

The slip is the money. The full voucher code is printed on the slip exactly once. A reprint requires authorisation. Handle unissued and issued slips like cash, because to whoever holds one, that is what it is. Hand the slip over with that sentence — customers keep them more carefully when told.

Locking the till. The padlock in the top bar locks the terminal:

• The shift stays open.
• The basket stays exactly as it is.
• Synchronisation continues in the background.
• Unlocking takes a username and password.

Lock the till every time you step away, even for a moment. It is faster than signing out and back in, it protects the open basket (the batch and serial work, the attached customer), and it protects you: an unattended, unlocked till trades under your name — its sales, its overrides and its variances become yours regardless of whose hands made them. On shared terminals, the lock is also how cashiers change over quickly between their own accounts (module 1's one-person-one-account rule).

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Closing the shift, and Okelewo's first month
lessons.html:
Closing the shift.

1. Click the clock icon. The Close Shift window shows the shift's totals — sales, returns, transaction count, and lay-by activity if there was any.
2. The counted-amount fields arrive pre-filled with what the system expects for each payment method. Do not accept these figures blindly.
3. Count the drawer and each method's takings. Overwrite each pre-filled figure with what you actually counted.
4. The variance appears beside each method — green for over, red for short — with a total at the bottom.
5. Explain any variance in the closing notes (for example: 200 over — suspected change error on a busy split sale around 4pm).
6. Click Close Shift. Duty turns Inactive.

Why not accept the pre-filled figures? The pre-fill is the system's expectation, not a count. Accepting it untouched just confirms the system against itself and proves nothing about the drawer. The counted close is what makes the shift's record real — and a variance explained in one sentence at close is far cheaper than the same variance investigated days later, when nobody remembers the busy split sale at 4pm.

Unclosed shifts. An unclosed shift leaves its sales unattributed until a supervisor reconciles them after the fact with the back-office orphaned-transactions tool. Report a missed close rather than hiding it — the tool exists as a correction, and the pattern is visible either way.

Okelewo's first month on shifts. Four events from the first month, each matching a chapter:

• Week 2 — the counted float pays off. The flagship's Tuesday drawer opens 1,500 short of the prepared float. Because the cashier counts and declares it in the opening note, the cause is found the same morning: the weekend crew had raided the float box for change. Fix: floats sealed after preparation. Under the old routine, the shortfall would have surfaced at close and been argued about for an hour.
• Week 3 — hold, not clear. A customer leaves to fetch a wallet mid-sale with three serials already scanned. The basket is held, not cleared; it resumes intact ten minutes later. Rebuilding it would have meant re-scanning the serials — or worse, guessing.
• The blind close, once. On a rushed Saturday a cashier accepts the pre-filled figures untouched. The supervisor spots it the same evening — untouched closes are recognisable by their perfect zeros — and the drawer is re-counted together: 350 over, real, unexplained because uncounted. The re-count teaches the lesson better than any memo.
• The split-payment pattern. One cashier shows small, consistent cash shortages on split-payment days. The variance report narrows it in minutes: transfers being rung as cash to balance faster — Chapter 6's exact warning. A five-minute retrain ends it. Note what the report did: it turned a suspicion into a specific, fixable habit, and cleared the cashier of anything worse.

The MD's month-end note: for nine years the drawers were about right. Now I know per shift, per person, per method — and the arguments have stopped. The counting turned out to be the cheap part.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Review & the fourth law
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section before the quiz.

Sign-in and the screen (Chapter 1). Normal, offline (this terminal, within seven days), and manager override (tagged for audit, cashier told). The top bar: Online/Offline, Offline login, Queued (safe, posts automatically), Re-login (that cashier's queued sales cannot post until they sign in online), Conflicts, Stock/Price stale, Failed, Duty and the shift button, Message Hub, Sync, the padlock, Sign out. Console layout: products left, order right, totals in the footer, consoles per your access row.

Opening (Chapter 2). Count the float physically; enter it per method; declare anything unusual in the opening note. The opening figure is what the close is measured against — a typed round number manufactures variances. Handover = two shifts, two counts. Never sell with Duty Inactive; orphaned sales need the back-office repair tool.

The cart (Chapter 3). Scan (no focus needed), search, or tap. Stack vs queue. Enter applies a quantity, Escape abandons it. Bonus, bundle-component and voucher lines are fixed; remove a bundle by its main line. Markers: Bundle, Rate override, Customer discount, Batch assigned. Ten-second footer check before payment.

Tracked items (Chapter 4). Batches: split allowed; auto-allocate picks oldest first; reductions release in reverse; the Batch assigned marker reviews the pick — make the record match the bag. Serials: one per unit, from the units in the bag, and the line will not reach payment without them. Units: the price follows the unit — check it. A refused batch/serial means another till took it: re-pick; a held-back sale shows under Conflicts.

Customers (Chapter 5). Attach by search, create (mobile-match auto-merge), or loyalty scan — before the first item when you can. Attaching applies recorded discounts and shows balance/limit. Over-limit shows Sales suspended; only a Credit Limit Override approver releases it; never split tickets around it. Earning needs attachment; redemption needs the server; returns recover spent points and show the figure first.

Payment (Chapter 6). Hold keeps everything; Clear discards and may need approval — hold, do not clear. Cash calculates change and opens the drawer. Split: each portion on its true method; over-tender only with cash in the mix. Server-verified tenders: loyalty, vouchers, store credit. Offline: collect the full amount. Back-dating: today or earlier, sparingly.

Receipts, vouchers, the lock (Chapter 7). Reprints from Recent receipts or Sales History. Offline local reference and the later invoice number find the same sale. Voucher sale: denomination, scan pre-printed cards, named customer, cash-equivalent tender only, and the slip is the money — the code prints once, reprints need authorisation. Lock every time you step away: shift open, basket kept, sync running, your name protected.

Closing (Chapter 8). Pre-filled figures are expectations, not counts: count, overwrite, explain. Green over, red short. Report missed closes.

The fourth law: the shift is a sealed routine — count at open, count at close, explain every variance. Module 5 covers discounts, returns and overrides.

concessions_returns.title: POS 5 — Concessions, Returns & Overrides
concessions_returns.desc: Everything that takes money off or gives money back: the concession event's five-part anatomy, the three discount modes as lived at the till, the markdown-reason craft with budget percentages, the discount-request code cycle end to end, promotions and bundles as the priced automatic concession, rate edits and credit releases under the override machinery, and the Return & Exchange console's three steps with loyalty recovery — generosity spent like the money it is.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The pressure valve: money off, money back
lessons.html:
Four modules built a counter that takes money correctly. This one governs the harder motion: money going the OTHER way — the discount, the rate cut, the credit release, the refund. The pressure-valve module, under the track's fifth law: every concession and every return carries a reason and an authoriser.

Why one module. The unification argued: discounts and returns look like different subjects — one is selling's generosity, the other service's obligation — but structurally they are ONE subject: authorised exceptions to the sale's normal arithmetic, sharing one control machinery (the Power Approver table, the override modes, the reason disciplines) and one risk shape (the exception path is where margin leaks and where fraud dresses as service — module 8's map draws most of its lines through this module's ground). The counter needs the valve — the shop that can never bend loses customers it should keep, and the damaged item genuinely is worth less — so the discipline is never 'no exceptions'; it is the law above: every exception a governed EVENT, with a reason that survives and an authoriser who owns it.

The event's anatomy. The shape every concession and return shares, taught once and recognised everywhere after: a SUBJECT (the line or invoice the exception touches), an ACTOR (the cashier proposing), an AUTHORISER (the approver disposing — by password or code, per the profile), a REASON (chosen, and in approval mode explained), and a TRAIL (the marker on the line, the stamp on the invoice, the timestamped stages of a request). Five parts; the module's every mechanism is one of them made concrete — and the diagnostic habit follows: the exception missing any part is the finding (the discount with no reason, the return with no invoice, the override with no approver are the trade's three commonest leaks, and each is a part of the anatomy amputated).

The module's map. The ground ahead: the three discount modes as lived at the till (Chapter 2 — module 2 chose them; this module works them), the markdown-reason craft that makes approval mode's data worth having (3), the code cycle's full walk (4), the promotion and bundle machinery that concedes AUTOMATICALLY so the till doesn't have to (5), the stronger powers — rate edits and credit releases — under the override machinery in action (6), the Return & Exchange console's three steps with the loyalty-recovery arithmetic (7), Okelewo's concession quarter (8), and the patterns and the law (9). One frame carries throughout, set now: the margin is a quantity the firm OWNS — every naira conceded is spent, and spending needs what spending always needs in this academy: an authoriser, a reason, and a record that lets the owner read where it went.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The three modes at the till: what the cashier lives
lessons.html:
Module 2 chose the discount mode as policy; this chapter is the same ground from the chair — what each mode feels like, line by line. The lived-modes chapter.

Standard mode. The direct path: the percentage icon on the line, the switch between percentage and amount, the discount entered — with the arithmetic fences known (a percentage cannot exceed one hundred; an amount cannot exceed the line's rate — the discount that inverts a price into a payment does not exist), and Apply. Where the profile requires an override, the approver clears it AT THE MOMENT of discounting — password typed, or a one-time code requested and entered. The mode's honest character restated from the chair: fast, floor-supervised, and exactly as governed as the approver's presence.

Approval-based mode. The same window with two additions that change everything: a discount reason chosen from the list, and a typed explanation — neither can be left blank. The reason is stored ON the sale line and surfaces in markdown reporting — which is the mode's whole point, felt at the till as thirty seconds of friction and read at month-end as the only margin report that answers WHY. The cashier's craft in this mode is honesty at speed: the reason picked is the TRUE one, not the top one (Chapter 3 owns why the list is short enough to make truth easy), and the explanation is a sentence a stranger can use ('display unit, box damaged, customer shown') — the discipline every evidence layer in this academy asks: written for the reader who wasn't there.

Code-based mode. The till's side of Chapter 4's cycle: the cashier CANNOT type a discount at all — Request Discount on the cart header instead: the item searched, the quantity set, percentage or amount chosen, the ask entered, submitted — then the wait, and on approval, the ticket icon on the line and the code entered. One rule at the line: a line already carrying a discount code cannot be discounted again — the code is the concession, whole.

What cannot be discounted. The refusal list, taught with its reasons because the tooltip will cite it: bonus items from a promotion (already free — a discount on free is a fiction), lines already carrying a promotional discount (the campaign locked the line — Chapter 5's stacking prevention), lines carrying a discount code (above), gift voucher lines (a voucher sells at face value, always — module 4's closed loop), and bundle components (the bundle price governs the parts). And the disabled control's grammar, closing the chapter as it closed module 1: the greyed discount control is HOVERED, and the tooltip states the reason — discounts disabled on the profile, a promotion or code already applied, or no approvers configured — the machine explaining its constitution so the cashier can explain it to the queue, which is the difference between a refusal and an argument, sixty times a week.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The markdown-reason craft: why the list is short
lessons.html:
Approval-based mode is only as good as its reason list — and the list is a designed instrument, not a form field. The craft chapter.

The list's discipline. The manual's design rules, adopted with their reasoning: the list SHORT and mutually exclusive — damaged stock, price match, display item, expiring stock and goodwill cover most shops — because a list of thirty reasons produces unusable data: cashiers pick the first plausible entry, every reason becomes 'other' wearing a costume, and the month-end report answers nothing. The design logic is the academy's category discipline (few buckets, purpose-clear, no overlaps) applied where the data is born under queue pressure: the reason pickable in two seconds AND true is the design target, and five well-cut reasons beat thirty precise ones every month of the year.

The budget percentage. The field that turns the list from taxonomy into control: each reason carries a budget percentage — the share of markdown budget it is EXPECTED to account for — letting finance compare planned against actual concessions. The read taught as module 8 will use it: the shop that budgeted damaged-stock at forty percent of markdowns and reads it running at seventy has a QUESTION (a receiving problem, a storage problem, or a reason being borrowed as the easy pick); goodwill budgeted at ten and running at forty is a floor-culture read; and price-match spiking in one branch is competitive intelligence arriving through the till. The budget line makes the markdown report a variance report — expectation against actual, per cause — which is this academy's epistemics (the reconciliation as the read) applied to generosity.

The empty-list trap. The commissioning rule, stated as the manual states it: in Approval-based mode, a discount cannot be applied at all if no markdown reasons exist — create them BEFORE switching a profile into the mode. The trap's shape is module 2's no-approvers pattern exactly (the required input with no supply — the control that becomes a wall), and it joins the go-live checklist beside it: the mode switch rehearsed with a real discounted sale, reason picked, explanation typed, override cleared, before the first customer meets it.

The analytics dividend. The chapter's closing argument, made to the owner: the reason discipline costs each discount thirty seconds and buys the firm the one report suspicion cannot fake — the margin's leak DECOMPOSED by cause, per branch, per cashier, per period, against budget. The Okelewo preview (Chapter 8 cashes it): the first quarter's markdown read replaced three standing arguments with three decisions — because 'we discount too much' is a mood, but 'expiring-stock markdowns doubled at the flagship in March, concentrated in provisions, eleven approvals, all one supplier's short-dated deliveries' is a purchasing conversation with a name on it. The reasons are the difference; the list's shortness is why the reasons are true; and the budget line is why the report reads itself.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The code cycle: negotiation, governed
lessons.html:
Code-based mode's machinery, walked end to end — the trade's counter negotiation, rebuilt as a governed cycle. The cycle chapter.

The five stages. The cycle as the manual gives it, each stage read for its control: (1) The request. At the till, Request Discount — the item searched, the quantity, the ask as a percentage or an amount per unit, submitted. The request is born as a DOCUMENT (the proposal on record before any answer — the anatomy's subject and actor, captured). (2) The routing. The request is created against the requesting BRANCH and routed to the category leads for that item's group — authority following the goods, not the org chart's nearest warm body: the person who owns electronics margin answers electronics asks, whichever branch asked. (3) The decision. A lead reviews in the back office and APPROVES — optionally CHANGING the amount (the counter asked for fifteen; the lead grants ten — the negotiation happening at the authoriser, recorded) — or REJECTS with the outcome recorded. (4) The code. An approved request carries a discount code; the cashier types it into the cart. (5) The application. Applying the code reserves it briefly against that cashier so two tills cannot consume the same approval, then marks it USED and stamps it against the resulting invoice. And over all five: every stage is timestamped with who did it — a complete audit trail from request to sale, which is the anatomy of Chapter 1 achieved in full: subject, actor, authoriser, reason, trail, each a database fact.

The routing's precondition. The setup rule with the manual's own warning: item groups must have category leads assigned on the request routing — without leads, requests have nobody to approve them: the no-approvers trap's third appearance (approvers, reasons, leads — the pattern the certified consultant now checks by reflex: every required-supply control staffed before the mode that requires it goes live), and the lead assignment is itself an authority-map decision (who owns this category's margin is answered in writing, per group).

The mode's economics. The judgment restated with the cycle visible: code-based buys the STRONGEST separation (the concession decided away from the counter's pressure, by the margin's owner, at review speed) at the cost of ROUND-TRIP latency (the customer waits, or returns) — which is why the mode suits high-value negotiated goods (the electronics wall, the furniture floor — one code per hour, each worth the wait) and punishes the provisions queue (thirty asks a day would queue the shop). The mixed estate runs mixed modes — module 2's profile-per-policy logic cashing here: Okelewo's pilot (Chapter 8) puts code-based on the Lagos electronics profile ONLY, approval-based everywhere else — and the certified consultant designs the split by the goods' negotiation reality, not by uniformity's tidiness. The chapter's closing line: the cycle is the trade's oldest counter ritual — 'oga, wetin be your last price' — answered not with a wall but with a governed channel: the ask recorded, the owner deciding, the code single-use, the invoice stamped. Negotiation survives; leakage doesn't.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Promotions & bundles: the automatic concession
lessons.html:
The machinery that concedes WITHOUT the till asking anyone — campaigns and bundles, governed at creation instead of at application. The automatic chapter.

The three promotion kinds. The catalogue: Product Discount (a percentage or fixed amount off qualifying lines), Bonus Item (a free item added to the basket — the bonus line uneditable and undiscountable at the till, per Chapter 2's refusal list), and Bonus Loyalty Points (extra points against a named programme, optionally with their own validity). Three shapes of generosity, all sharing the design property that makes them safe: the concession is DECIDED ONCE, centrally, by the campaign's owner — and applied by the machinery when the basket qualifies, identically at every till, with no counter judgment involved: cashiers do not have to remember campaigns, and campaigns cannot be 'remembered' generously.

Setting one up. The eight-step walk, each step a policy: the TITLE and DESCRIPTION (both visible to cashiers — written for the floor), Valid From and Valid To (outside the window the promotion is IGNORED even if active — the campaign that ends by calendar, not by memo: the expiring-access discipline of two tracks, applied to generosity), the TRIGGER (a specific item, an item group, a brand, or the transaction as a whole) with its subject named, the qualifying THRESHOLDS (minimum and maximum quantity for item-level triggers; minimum and maximum transaction value for basket-level ones — the maximums mattering: the promotion capped is the promotion whose worst case is priced), the REWARD defined (discount type and value, the bonus item, or the points and programme), the AUTOMATIC decision (applies itself, or carries a promotion code the cashier types — the tag icon above the grid, applied codes showing as removable chips on the footer), and the STATUS set Active.

Promotions lock the line. The stacking rule, taught as the control it is: once a promotional discount lands on a cart line, the cashier can no longer edit that line's rate or add a manual discount to it — preventing a manual concession stacked on top of a campaign. The design read: the promotion is a PRICED concession (the campaign's owner computed its cost); the stack would be an unpriced one (campaign plus counter generosity, compounding invisibly) — and the lock is the machinery refusing the compound, with the tooltip explaining it to the till.

Bundles. The grouped sale's machinery: a bundle names a main item, a bundle price, and the component items with quantities; at the till, adding the main item where a bundle exists offers the CHOICE — bundle or single — and choosing the bundle brings components in as indented child lines under the main line, with the governance known from module 4's cart: child lines' quantity, rate and discount are FIXED individually — the bundle price governs. And the lifecycle rule, small and load-bearing: set a bundle inactive rather than deleting if it may return — deleting loses the component list (disable-not-delete, at the bundle). The chapter's closing frame: promotions and bundles are the concession machinery at its safest — generosity designed, priced, windowed and locked in the back office, executed identically by every till — and the certified counter prefers them for exactly that reason: every campaign moved from 'the floor knows' to a record is a leak converted to a line item.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The stronger powers: rate edits & credit releases
lessons.html:
Two powers outrank the discount — rewriting the price itself, and releasing a suspended credit sale — and both live under the override machinery this chapter watches in action. The stronger-powers chapter.

The rate edit. The power and its governance: where the profile allows it, the pencil icon opens Edit Rate — the new unit price typed, the line thereafter marked Rate override so it is visible on review, and, where the require-override companion is on (module 2 called it near-mandatory), an approver clearing every change. The power's rank argued once: a discount is bounded by the rate (the amount cannot exceed it — Chapter 2's fence); the rate edit REPLACES the bound itself — it is the price list overruled at one line, the memory-price disease readmitted for one sale — which is why the marker exists (the overridden line announces itself to module 8's reader), why the override companion is the default posture, and why the rate-edit pattern per cashier is a standing supervision read (the till whose Tuesday sales carry a dozen Rate override markers has a story to tell, and the marker means it will be told).

The credit release. Module 4's suspend, resolved: the cart showing Sales suspended due to customer outstanding unblocks only through a Power Approver holding the credit-limit permission — and the release is read as the credit DECISION it is: the approver is not waving a screen past; they are extending the firm's exposure beyond its recorded limit, on their name, for this sale — the Selling track's credit governance executed in one prompt, and the release pattern (which customers, how often, released by whom) is the counter's contribution to the receivables conversation: the customer released weekly is a limit that needs re-deciding, one way or the other, by credit's owner rather than by the till's momentum.

The override machinery in action. The prompt's mechanics, gathered once for the whole module: the approver's email and password typed at the till — or the one-time code path per the action's override mode: the code REQUESTED (the terminal must be online), six digits emailed to every approver holding the relevant permission, valid for one hour, entered at the prompt. The troubleshooting inherited from the manual: the code that never arrives is an approver with no email address, a terminal that was offline at request time, or a code past its hour — request a fresh one. And the design's audit property restated as this module's spine: the all-holders email means every override REQUEST is announced to the whole approver group — the quiet arrangement between one cashier and one soft approver is structurally noisy — and the completed override is an event (who approved, what, when) that module 8's page counts by type and by approver: the approver whose password clears forty discounts a week is either the floor's whole valve (a staffing read) or its rubber stamp (a governance read), and the counting is what tells which. The chapter's closing line: the stronger powers are exactly where the anatomy of Chapter 1 earns its keep — the actor proposing, the authoriser owning, the marker surviving — because the price rewritten and the credit extended are the two concessions the margin and the balance sheet feel directly.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Return & Exchange: money's reverse gear, in three steps
lessons.html:
The console the profile revealed (module 2's visibility rule) and the module's second half: the return, walked as the three-step, policy-aware flow the product builds. The returns chapter.

Step one — Find Invoice. The return BEGINS at the original sale, always: the receipt barcode scanned, or the reference typed — the till reference or the back-office invoice number, either working (module 4's two-reference law cashing at the desk), multiple matches offering a choice — and the invoice SUMMARY read before anything is built: its date, outstanding amount, item count, and whether it is still within the return window. The step's law is module 1's inheritance made procedural: no invoice, no return — the phantom return's first wall — and the summary's window flag telling the cashier NOW whether this return is routine or needs the out-of-window override, before the conversation deepens.

Step two — Build Return. The two shapes: REFUND — the lines and quantities coming back selected, a REASON chosen from the list (defective item, wrong item delivered, customer changed mind, damaged in transit, quality issues, size or colour issue, or other — the fixed vocabulary that makes returns reporting readable, the markdown-list logic at the returns desk), and the money's route chosen: Store Credit, or Cash Refund — with cash appearing ONLY if the profile permits it (Okelewo's launch posture shows store credit alone, by design). EXCHANGE — as above, plus the replacement goods searched and added, the DIFFERENCE computed both ways: the customer owing more chooses a payment method for the balance; the customer owed chooses the refund method. And the tracked-goods gate: returning a serial-numbered item asks which serials are coming back — the identity law running in reverse, the unit returned being the unit sold.

Step three — Complete. The authorisation and the paper: where the profile requires it, the approver clears the return — password or one-time code, per the return override mode — the return POSTS, and a return or exchange receipt prints. The event whole: subject (the found invoice), actor, authoriser, reason, trail — the anatomy, at the desk where it matters most.

Loyalty recovery. The arithmetic the product does so the cashier doesn't guess: where the original sale EARNED points that have since been SPENT, the system works out how much must be recovered and adds it to what the customer owes — shown before completion, so the cashier explains it from the screen. The design's point taught: the return that refunds the goods but ignores the spent points quietly pays the customer twice (the refund plus the points' value already redeemed) — the recovery closes the loop, and the certified cashier's script treats it as the system's fairness, visible and explainable, not a negotiation.

The connection rule. The console's honest limit: Return & Exchange is unreachable while the terminal is offline — the return needs the server (the original invoice, the loyalty ledger, the credit balance all live there) — so the offline counter takes the customer's details or asks them to return when the line is back: the same balance-verification honesty as store credit, at the desk. The chapter's closing frame: the console's whole shape — find first, reason always, route by policy, authorise where required, recover the points, need the line — is the fifth law implemented as software; the certified professional's job is running it as designed and reading what it records.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: Okelewo's concession quarter
lessons.html:
Ninety days of governed generosity — the modes at work, the data arriving, and the first hard returns. Every chapter clocks in.

The markdown data's first read (Ch. 2-3). Approval-based mode has run at all three branches for a quarter, and the first serious markdown review replaces moods with names, exactly as promised: EXPIRING-STOCK markdowns run double budget at the flagship — decomposed in twenty minutes to eleven approvals, all provisions, all one supplier's short-dated deliveries (a purchasing conversation, held that week, with the report on the table); GOODWILL runs under budget everywhere except one Lagos cashier whose explanations read thin ('customer asked' three times — a coaching conversation, not an accusation: the explanations were read because they exist); and PRICE MATCH spikes in Abeokuta the week a competitor opens — competitive intelligence through the till, priced. The MD's margin argument with himself, standing since module 1, ends: the leak has causes, the causes have owners, and two of three arguments become decisions.

The code-based pilot (Ch. 4). The Lagos electronics wall goes code-based per the economics: the category lead assigned (the precondition checked — the leads exist BEFORE the mode switches), and the first month's cycle data reads clean — nineteen requests, fourteen approved (six with the amount CHANGED down by the lead — the negotiation moved to the margin's owner, visibly), five rejected with outcomes recorded, every code single-use and stamped. One designed refusal earns its keep: a cashier attempts to reuse a morning's code on an afternoon sale — consumed, refused, and the attempt itself a read (a training note, this time; the reserved-against-cashier design meanwhile having made the two-till double-spend structurally impossible).

A promotion, priced and locked (Ch. 5). The first campaign — provisions basket discount, windowed two weeks, transaction-triggered with a maximum — runs without a single till decision: the lock survives its test when a cashier tries to add goodwill on top of a promoted line (refused, tooltip read aloud to the queue, no argument), and the campaign closes BY ITS WINDOW while the old counter's habit — the promo that lingers by memory for a month — dies quietly. The bundle machinery launches with the season's hamper: main item, bundle price, components indented and fixed, and the January decision made properly — the hamper set INACTIVE, not deleted, its component list preserved for next year.

The returns quarter (Ch. 6-7). The desk's three firsts: the first OUT-OF-WINDOW return (day thirty-four, defective kettle) walks the designed path — the summary flags the lapsed window at find-invoice, the supervisor's override clears it with the reason on record, and the desk learns the difference between a wall and a governed gate; the first LOYALTY RECOVERY is explained from the screen (the customer's spent points computed into what she owes, shown before completion — one raised eyebrow, zero disputes, because the number was the system's and visible); and the RATE-OVERRIDE read catches the quarter's one real governance item — a flagship till's Friday sales carrying repeated Rate override markers, traced to one senior cashier 'matching' prices from memory for regulars: the require-override companion switched on for that profile the same week (module 2's near-mandatory posture, adopted the moment its absence was read). At ninety days the CASH-REFUND decision comes due as scheduled: the quarter's returns data (volumes low, reasons clean, overrides working) supports enabling cash refunds at the flagship only — override required, drawer impact briefed to module 8's close ritual — store credit remaining the default elsewhere: the conservative posture relaxed by evidence, not by sympathy. The MD's quarter note: we gave away less, argued less, and I can read where every conceded naira went. The valve works better than the wall did.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fifth law
lessons.html:
The valve's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the amputated event. Symptom: discounts with no reason, returns with no invoice, overrides with no approver; the exception path as the leak path. Disease: the anatomy incomplete (Ch. 1). Fix: five parts, always — subject, actor, authoriser, reason, trail — and the missing part treated as the finding.

Pattern 2 — the thirty-reason list. Symptom: every markdown filed under the first plausible entry; month-end data that answers nothing; 'other' wearing costumes. Disease: taxonomy built for completeness instead of truth-at-speed (Ch. 3). Fix: five mutually exclusive reasons with budget percentages — short enough to pick honestly in two seconds, budgeted so the report reads itself.

Pattern 3 — the unstaffed control. Symptom: approval mode with no reasons; overrides with no approvers; code mode with no category leads — the wall where a gate was designed. Disease: required supply not staffed before the requiring mode (Ch. 3-4). Fix: the reflex check — reasons, approvers, leads created and rehearsed on the go-live list before any mode that needs them switches on.

Pattern 4 — the stacked concession. Symptom: campaign discounts with manual generosity on top; promotions whose real cost nobody priced; the compound leak. Disease: concessions allowed to combine unpriced (Ch. 5). Fix: the lock respected as designed — promotions lock the line, codes are the whole concession, and every campaign carries its window and its maximums.

Pattern 5 — the unmarked rewrite. Symptom: prices 'matched' from memory line by line; rate edits without overrides; the memory-price disease back through the pencil icon. Disease: the strongest power under the weakest governance (Ch. 6). Fix: require-override on wherever rate editing is allowed, the Rate override marker read per cashier per week, and the pattern answered the week it appears.

Pattern 6 — the sympathetic return. Symptom: refunds without the invoice found; cash out of the drawer on a wave; spent loyalty points refunded twice; the window ignored because the customer was insistent. Disease: service instincts overriding the machinery (Ch. 7). Fix: the three steps as designed — find first, reason always, route by policy, authorise where required, recover the points — with the out-of-window override as the governed mercy the design already provides.

The fifth law. The valve, governed: every concession and every return carries a reason and an authoriser — the modes worked as chosen, the reason lists short and budgeted, the cycle staffed, promotions priced windowed and locked, the stronger powers marked and counted, and the return built on its found invoice with the points recovered — generosity spent like the money it is. Module 6 opens the extended counters: Lay-By, Staff Purchase, Airtime and the Customer Desk — money in its other costumes.
